goals: Name the three ruling families and describe the tradition of the Sangams as a tradition
Explain what Sangam literature and the Tirukkural tell us, without quoting any poem
Explain what megalithic burials and their grave goods suggest about early South Indian society
Describe the position of women in Sangam society, including women poets

slides.heading: The Sangam Age: kingdoms, sources and women
slides.body_md: Part 1 — who ruled, how we know about the age, and how women appear in the sources.

slides.narration: The Sangam Age is usually placed from about the third century before the common era to about the third century of the common era. Books vary, so always say about. The date of the Tirukkural is debated. It is often placed somewhere between about the first century before the common era and the fifth century of the common era.

slides.heading: Three ruling families

visual.alt: Table of the three ruling families: the Cheras on the west coast with the port of Muziris and pepper, the Cholas in the Kaveri region with the port of Puhar and fertile farmland, and the Pandyas in the Madurai area with the port of Korkai, pearls and the tradition of the Sangams

slides.narration: Three ruling families are named in the sources. The Cheras were linked with the west coast and the port of Muziris. The Cholas were linked with the Kaveri region and the port of Puhar. The Pandyas were linked with the Madurai area and the port of Korkai, which was known for pearls.

slides.heading: The three Sangams: a tradition
bullets: Tradition speaks of **three Sangams**, assemblies of **poets**.
They are said to have met at **Madurai** under **Pandya patronage**.
Treat this as **tradition**, not as established fact.

nodes.label: Held at Madurai under Pandya patronage
A tradition, not a proved fact

visual.alt: Flow: tradition speaks of three Sangams of poets, held at Madurai under Pandya patronage; this is tradition and not a fully proved fact
visual.caption: The three Sangams: tradition.

slides.narration: Tradition speaks of three Sangams, which were assemblies of poets. They are said to have met at Madurai under the patronage of the Pandya kings. In an exam we present this as tradition. The details are not fully proved, and we do not state them as established fact.

slides.body_md: Which list names the three ruling families of the Sangam Age?
slides.narration: Think about the table you have just seen. Which three families ruled in the Tamil region?

slides.heading: Sangam literature
slides.body_md: The works tell us about **kings, war, trade, landscapes and daily life**.

rows: Later epics, usually placed just after the Sangam period

visual.alt: Table of Sangam literature: the Tolkappiyam on grammar, the Ettuthogai or Eight Anthologies, the Pattuppattu or Ten Idylls, and the later epics Silappatikaram and Manimekalai usually placed just after the Sangam period

slides.narration: Sangam literature includes the Tolkappiyam, a work on grammar. It also includes the Ettuthogai, the Eight Anthologies, and the Pattuppattu, the Ten Idylls. Two later epics, the Silappatikaram and the Manimekalai, are usually placed just after the Sangam period. We only name them here.

slides.heading: What the literature tells us
bullets: It tells us about **kings and war**, **trade**, **landscapes** and **daily life**.
Poets often **praised their patrons**: read with care.
Compare with **other evidence**, such as excavations.

nodes.label: Kings, war, trade, landscapes, daily life
Read with care, with other evidence

visual.alt: Flow: the poems and other works tell us about kings, war, trade, landscapes and daily life, and are read with care and with other evidence
visual.caption: What the literature tells us.

slides.narration: The poems and other works tell us about kings and war, about trade, about the landscapes of the region and about daily life. But poets often praised the people who supported them. A historian therefore reads such works with care and compares them with other evidence, such as the results of excavations.

slides.heading: The Tirukkural: key facts
slides.body_md: We describe its structure and themes only; we **never quote** a couplet.

rows: Debated; often placed about 1st century BCE to 5th century CE
A guide to ethics and conduct

visual.alt: Table of facts on the Tirukkural: attributed to Thiruvalluvar, 1,330 couplets in 133 chapters of ten, date debated and often placed about the 1st century BCE to the 5th century CE, valued as a guide to ethics and conduct

slides.narration: The Tirukkural is attributed to Thiruvalluvar. It has one thousand three hundred and thirty couplets, called kurals, arranged in one hundred and thirty three chapters of ten. Its date is debated, and it is valued as a guide to ethics and conduct. In exams we describe its themes and never quote its lines.

slides.heading: Three parts, three themes
bullets: **Aram:** virtue.
**Porul:** wealth and polity (government).
**Inbam:** love.

visual.alt: Flow of the three parts of the Tirukkural: aram or virtue, porul or wealth and polity, and inbam or love
visual.caption: The three parts of the Tirukkural.

slides.narration: The Tirukkural has three parts. Aram deals with virtue. Porul deals with wealth and polity, which means government and the management of wealth. Inbam deals with love. Together they give a guide to right conduct in personal life, public life and family life.

slides.heading: Quick check: parts in order
slides.body_md: Arrange the three parts of the Tirukkural in the usual order.
slides.narration: Start with virtue, then wealth and polity, and finish with love.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: choosing the right source
slides.body_md: Ask what you want to know, then pick the source that fits.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the question the historian is asking.
Step 2 — Decide: conduct, grammar, kings and trade, or burials?
Step 3 — Match it with a work or a burial site.
Step 4 — Add one more kind of evidence and note its limits.

rows: What did people think about conduct and virtue?
What were ports, kings and landscapes like?
The anthologies and idylls, with other evidence
How were the dead buried and with what goods?

visual.alt: Table matching four historian questions with sources: conduct and virtue in the Tirukkural, grammar in the Tolkappiyam, ports kings and landscapes in the anthologies and idylls with other evidence, and burials in megalithic sites

slides.narration: Here is a simple method. Read the question and decide whether it is about conduct, grammar, kings and trade, or burials. Then match it with a source. Questions on conduct go to the Tirukkural. Grammar goes to the Tolkappiyam. Burials go to megalithic sites. Always add one more kind of evidence and note its limits.

slides.heading: Megaliths: burials marked with big stones

rows: A ring of large stones marking a burial
A chamber of large stones with a capstone
A box-like grave lined with stone slabs
Remains in a large pottery urn; Adichanallur is a well-known site

visual.alt: Table of megalithic burials: a stone circle is a ring of large stones, a dolmen a chamber of large stones with a capstone, a cist a box-like grave lined with slabs, and an urn burial holds remains in a large pottery urn, as at Adichanallur

slides.narration: Megaliths are burials marked with large stones. A stone circle is a ring of stones. A dolmen is a chamber of large stones with a capstone. A cist is a box shaped grave lined with slabs. In an urn burial the remains are placed in a large pottery urn. Adichanallur in Tamil Nadu is a well known urn burial site.

slides.heading: What the grave goods suggest
bullets: **Iron** tools and weapons **suggest** the use of iron.
Black-and-red pottery and ornaments **suggest** a belief in life after death.
Unequal goods **suggest** differences in status.

rows: Goods placed for the dead: a belief in life after death
Many goods in one grave, few in another

visual.alt: Table of grave goods and what they suggest: iron tools and weapons suggest the use of iron, black-and-red pottery and ornaments suggest a belief in life after death, and many goods in one grave and few in another suggest differences in status

slides.narration: Burials contain goods such as iron tools and weapons, black and red pottery and ornaments. Iron tools suggest that the community used iron. Goods placed with the dead suggest a belief in life after death. Many goods in one grave and few in another suggest differences in status. We say suggest, because burials give only part of the picture.

slides.heading: Women poets
bullets: Women poets contributed to Sangam literature.
**Avvaiyar** is the best known; **Nachchellaiyar** and **Kakkaipadiniyar** are others.
A name shared by **more than one poet** in different periods: **Avvaiyar**.

nodes.label: Used by more than one poet across periods

visual.alt: Flow: the name Avvaiyar was used by more than one poet across periods, so a historian says which poet is meant
visual.caption: A name used by more than one poet.

slides.narration: Women poets contributed to Sangam literature. Avvaiyar is the best known. Nachchellaiyar and Kakkaipadiniyar are other names. The name Avvaiyar was used by more than one poet across different periods, so a careful historian says which poet is meant. The presence of women poets suggests that some women were educated.

slides.heading: Women in society
slides.body_md: The sources show a **mixed picture** of the lives of women.

rows: The poems describe the difficult lives of widows

visual.alt: Table on women in Sangam society: poets Avvaiyar, Nachchellaiyar and Kakkaipadiniyar, work in farming spinning weaving and selling goods, education suggested by the women poets, and the hardships of widows described in the poems

slides.narration: Besides poetry, women took part in farming, spinning and weaving, and selling goods. The poems also describe the hardships faced by widows, so the picture is a mixed one. The sources are poems written by particular poets, so they show part of the picture and must be read with care.

slides.body_md: True or false: women poets such as Avvaiyar contributed to Sangam literature.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a 10-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: (i) Name three works of Sangam literature. [3] (ii) Describe the Tirukkural. [3] (iii) What do they tell us? One caution. [4]
bullets: (i) Three works named in one line each.
(ii) Couplets and chapters, then three parts.
(iii) What they tell us, then one caution.
Aim for one point per mark.

rows: Three works named: Tolkappiyam, Ettuthogai, Pattuppattu
Couplets and chapters; three parts; themes
What the works tell us; one caution

visual.alt: Table planning a ten-mark answer on Sangam literature: part (i) three works for 3 marks, part (ii) the structure of the Tirukkural for 3 marks, part (iii) what the works tell us and a caution for 4 marks

slides.narration: To plan a ten mark answer in three parts, give three points to the first part, three to the second and four to the last. Part one names three works. Part two gives the structure of the Tirukkural and its three parts. Part three says what the works tell us and ends with one caution.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Ruling families: **Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas**; the three **Sangams** are a **tradition**.
Literature: **Tolkappiyam**, **Ettuthogai**, **Pattuppattu**; later epics named only.
**Tirukkural:** 1,330 couplets, **aram, porul, inbam**; date debated.
**Megaliths** suggest iron use, belief and status; **women** as poets and workers.

slides.narration: To sum up. The Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas ruled. The three Sangams are a tradition. Sangam literature and the Tirukkural tell us about kings, trade, landscapes and conduct, but we read them with care. Megalithic burials suggest the use of iron, a belief in life after death and differences in status. Women appear as poets and workers.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Say **about** with every date; books differ.
Present the three Sangams as **tradition**.
**Never quote** a poem or a couplet; describe themes.
Use **suggests** for what burials show.
Mention that **Avvaiyar** was a name used by more than one poet.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Add the word about to every date. Present the three Sangams as a tradition. Never quote a poem or a couplet, but describe its themes. Use the word suggests for what burials show. And remember that Avvaiyar was a name used by more than one poet.

slides.narration: The poems describe five landscapes called tinai. Kurinji is the hills. Mullai is forest and pasture. Marutam is farmland, and it was the most fertile. Neytal is the coast. Palai is dry land that is hard to farm. The five are a way the poems describe places, and real places often mix them.

slides.heading: Crops of the Sangam Age

rows: The main crop; grown on marutam farmland
Cash crops; cotton cloth was exported

visual.alt: Table of crops: rice the main crop on marutam farmland, sugarcane and cotton as cash crops with cotton cloth exported, millets in drier areas, and spices such as pepper ginger turmeric and cardamom with pepper prized overseas

slides.narration: Rice was the main crop. Sugarcane and cotton were also grown, and cotton cloth was a valued product. Millets grew in drier areas. Spices such as pepper, ginger, turmeric and cardamom were grown too, and pepper was especially prized overseas. Together these crops fed people and supplied the markets.

slides.heading: Irrigation: tanks and rivers
bullets: Fields were watered from **tanks** and **rivers**.
Channels carried water to the **rice** fields.
A **surplus** of food could go to markets.

nodes.label: Rivers and tanks store and carry water

slides.narration: Farmers watered their fields from tanks and rivers. Tanks stored water, and channels carried it to the fields. With dependable water, rice grew well, and farmers had a surplus that could go to the markets. Without irrigation, such a surplus would have been much smaller.

slides.heading: The Kallanai

visual.caption: The Kallanai: a traditional attribution.

slides.narration: The Kallanai, also called the Grand Anicut, is a stone dam on the Kaveri river. It is traditionally attributed to the Chola king Karikala, and it is dated about the second century of the common era. We say traditionally attributed because the attribution rests on tradition.

slides.heading: From field to overseas trade

visual.alt: Flow: farmers grow rice and cotton, surplus goes to markets, some goods reach the ports, and overseas trade follows
visual.caption: From field to overseas trade.

slides.narration: Farming was linked with trade. Farmers grew rice and cotton. A surplus went to the markets. Some goods, especially cotton cloth and spices, reached the ports. From the ports they went overseas. In this way the field, the market and the port were linked in one economy.

**Markets** in towns and ports.

slides.narration: Internal trade was carried on by barter and in markets. In barter, goods were exchanged for goods, as when rice was traded for cloth. Markets in towns and ports sold many goods. sections.heading: 1. The age and the three kingdoms
sections.body_md:
- The **Sangam Age** is placed about the **3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE**; books vary, so say **about**.

sections.heading: 2. Sangam literature and the Tirukkural
sections.body_md:
- **Tolkappiyam:** a work on grammar. **Ettuthogai:** the Eight Anthologies. **Pattuppattu:** the Ten Idylls.
- The later epics **Silappatikaram** and **Manimekalai** are usually placed just after the Sangam period (named only).
- The works tell us about **kings, war, trade, landscapes and daily life**; poets often praised patrons, so read with care.
- **Tirukkural:** attributed to **Thiruvalluvar**; **1,330 couplets (kurals)** in **133 chapters** of ten; three parts: **aram** (virtue), **porul** (wealth and polity), **inbam** (love). Its date is debated, often placed about the 1st century BCE to the 5th century CE. It is valued as a guide to ethics and conduct.
- Never quote a poem or a couplet; describe themes.

sections.heading: 3. Megaliths
sections.body_md:
- **Megaliths** are burials marked with **large stones**: **stone circles**, **dolmens**, **cists** and **urn burials** (**Adichanallur** in Tamil Nadu is a well-known urn-burial site).
- Grave goods include **iron tools and weapons**, **black-and-red pottery** and **ornaments**.
- They **suggest** the use of iron, a belief in life after death, and differences in status shown by grave goods. Burials give only part of the picture, so read them with literature.

Objects placed in a grave with the dead.

- **Crops:** **rice** (main), **sugarcane**, **cotton**, **millets**, and spices: **pepper**, ginger, turmeric, cardamom.

sections.heading: 6. Trade, ports and the Roman world
sections.body_md:
- **Internal trade:** barter and markets. **Overseas trade:** with the **Roman world, South-East Asia and West Asia**.
- **Ports:** **Puhar/Kaveripattinam** (Chola), **Muziris** (Chera, Kerala coast), **Korkai** (Pandya; pearls), **Arikamedu** near Puducherry (Indo-Roman site excavated in the 1940s).
- **Exports:** pepper, other spices, pearls, ivory, fine cotton cloth, precious stones. **Imports:** Roman gold and silver coins, wine in amphorae, glass, metals.
- **Yavanas:** Greeks, Romans and other West Asian traders. **Monsoon winds** helped sailing.
- **Evidence:** hoards of Roman coins; Arikamedu; the **Periplus of the Erythraean Sea** (1st century CE Greek guide for sailors; named only).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about.
- Stating the three Sangams as proved fact.
- Quoting a poem, a kural or the Periplus.
- Writing "the Kallanai was built by Karikala" without "traditionally attributed".
- Mixing up exports and imports, or Puhar, Muziris and Korkai.
- Writing that women of the Sangam Age had no part in learning or work.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a caution or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A guide at an imagined museum of South Indian history lists the three ruling families of the Sangam Age on a wall panel. Which list is on the panel?

options.text_md: The Mauryas, the Guptas and the Cholas
The Cheras, the Cholas and the Pandyas
The Pallavas, the Satavahanas and the Kushanas
The Cheras, the Mauryas and the Vakatakas

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Cheras, the Cholas and the Pandyas. The three ruling families named in Sangam literature were the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas. The Mauryas, Guptas, Satavahanas, Kushanas and Vakatakas ruled elsewhere or in other ages.

questions.stem_md: A teacher in an imagined school at Madurai says, "Tradition speaks of three Sangams." Which statement presents this correctly for a history exam?

options.text_md: Historians have proved every detail of three Sangams with dated records
The Sangams were meetings of kings from the north
The Sangams were markets where goods were bartered
Tradition says assemblies of poets met at Madurai under Pandya patronage; it is a tradition, not a fully proved fact

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Tradition says assemblies of poets met at Madurai under Pandya patronage; it is a tradition, not a fully proved fact. The Sangams are remembered as assemblies of poets under Pandya patronage, but the details come from tradition. They were not proved in full, they were not northern kings, and they were not markets.

questions.stem_md: A librarian in an imagined town library shelves a work of 1,330 couplets in 133 chapters of ten couplets each. To whom is this work attributed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Thiruvalluvar. The Tirukkural is attributed to Thiruvalluvar. Avvaiyar was a woman poet, Karikala was a Chola king, and the other name is not the attributed author of the Tirukkural.

questions.stem_md: A student club in the imagined Kaveripur school is sorting chapters of the Tirukkural by theme. A chapter on how a ruler should govern and how wealth should be managed would go under which part?

options.text_md: Porul, the part on wealth and polity
None, since the work has no parts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Porul, the part on wealth and polity. Governance and wealth belong to porul. Aram is virtue and inbam is love. The work has three parts, so it does have parts.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined history quiz, a contestant says, "The Tirukkural was certainly written in the year 50 BCE." Which reply is the most accurate?

options.text_md: Correct, because every scholar agrees on 50 BCE
Wrong, because it was written in the 20th century
Its date is debated; it is often placed somewhere between about the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE
Wrong, because the Tirukkural is not a literary work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its date is debated; it is often placed somewhere between about the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE. Scholars differ on when the Tirukkural was composed, so a single exact year cannot be claimed. It is not a modern work, and it is a literary work.

questions.stem_md: A card in an imagined gallery reads: "An early work of Tamil grammar, studied by poets." Which Sangam-age work does the card describe?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Tolkappiyam. The Tolkappiyam is the work on grammar. The Pattuppattu is the collection of ten idylls, and the Silappatikaram and Manimekalai are epics usually placed just after the Sangam period.

questions.stem_md: A student writes that the Silappatikaram and the Manimekalai are Sangam works in the strict sense. How should a careful historian correct this?

options.text_md: They are the oldest works of the Sangam Age
They are books on grammar like the Tolkappiyam
They are anthologies of eight books
They are later epics, usually placed just after the Sangam period

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They are later epics, usually placed just after the Sangam period. The two epics are usually placed just after the Sangam period. They are not the oldest works, not grammar, and the eight anthologies are the Ettuthogai.

questions.stem_md: An imagined poem of the Sangam style praises a chief for feeding every visiting poet. What caution should a historian keep in mind before using it as evidence?

options.text_md: Poems can never be used as evidence
Poets often praised their patrons, so the poem should be checked against other evidence
The poem must be accepted word for word
A poem can only tell us about the weather

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Poets often praised their patrons, so the poem should be checked against other evidence. Poets who depended on patrons tended to praise them, so a careful historian cross-checks. Poems are useful, though not to be accepted word for word, and they tell us about much more than weather.

questions.stem_md: Archaeologists in an imagined survey of Karuvur hills find a ring of large standing stones that marks a burial. What is this kind of megalith called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A stone circle. A ring of standing stones marking a burial is a stone circle. A dolmen is a chamber of large stones with a capstone, which is a different form; a cave and a tower are not burials.

questions.stem_md: Excavators of an imagined stone-circle burial at Kalinagar find an iron blade, black-and-red pots and a few ornaments. What does this best suggest?

options.text_md: The community knew nothing about metals
The community used iron and may have believed in some form of life after death
The burial belongs to a Roman merchant who sailed from Rome
The pots prove that the people never farmed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The community used iron and may have believed in some form of life after death. Iron tools and goods placed with the dead suggest the use of iron and a belief that the dead needed such things. They do not show ignorance of metals, a Roman burial, or that no one farmed.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined excavation, one cist contains only a few pots, while another in the same field contains many ornaments, iron weapons and a horse-like figurine. What can a historian cautiously say?

options.text_md: The two burials prove the community had no social differences
The ornaments show the buried person was a Chola king
The difference suggests differences in wealth or status within the community
Only the burial with pots is real

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The difference suggests differences in wealth or status within the community. Different quantities and kinds of grave goods suggest differences in status, though a careful historian says "suggests". They do not prove equality, do not name a king, and both burials are real.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Black-and-red pottery is commonly found among the grave goods of megalithic burials.

**Reason (R):** The presence of such pottery proves that every buried person was a ruler.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: black-and-red ware is a typical grave good. R is false: pottery cannot prove rank, and many ordinary burials contain it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Tirukkural has 1,330 couplets.

**Reason (R):** The Tirukkural is divided into three parts: aram, porul and inbam.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

(ii) **Exports:** pepper, other spices, pearls, ivory, fine cotton cloth and precious stones. **Imports:** Roman gold and silver coins, wine in amphorae, glass and metals.

(iii) **Internal trade** by **barter and markets** moved goods between landscapes; **overseas trade** linked the region with the **Roman world, South-East Asia and West Asia**, helped by the **monsoon winds**. An imagined trader's ledger of Puhar lists pepper, pearls and cotton cloth sent out, and Roman coins, wine in amphorae and glass brought in.

(i) Say which entries are exports and which are imports. **[3]**
(ii) Name two ports that could appear in such a ledger and the people called Yavanas. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the monsoon winds and the ports helped the trade, and what the Roman coins found in South India suggest. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Exports and imports; ports and Yavanas; monsoon and coins.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Exports:** pepper, pearls and fine cotton cloth. **Imports:** Roman gold and silver coins, wine in amphorae and glass.

(ii) **Puhar** (Chola) and **Muziris** (Chera) could appear. **Yavanas** was the term for **Greeks, Romans and other West Asian traders**.

(iii) The **monsoon winds** let sailors cross the sea in season, and **ports** gave ships a place to load and unload. Hoards of **Roman gold and silver coins** found in South India **suggest** that goods were exchanged with the **Roman world** in a flourishing two-way trade. Such a ledger therefore shows how a port town brought together local producers, markets and foreign traders, and why ports such as Puhar and Muziris grew rich.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined student claims: "Because poems praise kings and traders, nothing in Sangam literature can be trusted as history."

(i) Name three kinds of information that Sangam literature gives. **[3]**
(ii) Name two other kinds of evidence, apart from literature, for the period. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the claim: how far is it fair, and how should a historian use poems and other evidence together? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Information; other evidence; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Sangam literature tells us about **kings and war**, **trade**, **landscapes (tinai)** and **daily life**, including the lives of **women**.

(ii) **Megalithic burials** and their grave goods, and **excavated sites** such as **Arikamedu** with **Roman coin hoards**.

(iii) The claim is **partly fair**: poets often **praised patrons**, so some details may be **exaggerated**. But the poems also give **useful detail**, and they can be **checked against** burials, coins and excavations. A historian therefore uses **literature and archaeology together**, noting the **limits** of each and saying **about** with dates. In this way the student is right to be careful, but wrong to reject all the evidence, because a balanced historian weighs every source instead of trusting or discarding it entirely.
